intro: We design and build house extensions across Essex, from single storey kitchen extensions to full double storey additions. One team handles the design, the drawings, the planning, the building regulations and the build, so you deal with the same people from the first visit to the finished room.

Essex is a county of real variety, and that shapes how you extend in it. A Victorian villa on the London commuter fringe, a weatherboarded cottage in a historic market town, a family home in Chelmsford and a large detached house out towards Epping Forest all call for a different approach. We plan each extension around the house it is joining.

sideReturn.title: Planning permission for extensions in Essex
paragraphs: This is where local knowledge earns its keep, because Essex is not a single planning authority.

Householder planning is handled by your district, borough or city council, not by Essex County Council. That means Epping Forest, Brentwood, Chelmsford, Uttlesford, Harlow and so on, each with its own local plan. Southend-on-Sea and Thurrock are separate unitary councils. Worth knowing: from April 2028 these councils are being replaced by five new unitary authorities, and Epping Forest, which covers Buckhurst Hill, Chigwell and Loughton, becomes part of West Essex Council. The rules will not change overnight, but the name on the letterhead will.
Many extensions fall under permitted development and need no application, but large parts of Essex carry protections that reduce or remove those rights:

The Metropolitan Green Belt covers much of south and west Essex, including the Epping Forest district. In the Green Belt you can still extend, but the scale is limited, so the work is not a disproportionate addition to the original house.

items.title: Ground
items.text: Essex has genuinely varied ground, and it changes what your foundations need to do.

items.title: Access
items.text: Much of the south and the London fringe sits on London Clay, which swells and shrinks with the seasons and moves most near mature trees, so foundations often go deeper there. Across the central and northern plateau the ground is boulder clay, a stiff but variable glacial deposit that can change over a short distance. The far north west, up towards Saffron Walden, runs onto chalk, while the river valleys and the coast bring softer gravels, alluvium and made ground. On the Epping Forest ridge, sandier beds cap the clay on the higher ground.

items.title: Neighbours
items.text: None of this is a problem when it is understood before work begins. It is a problem when it is not. A builder who knows the local ground designs the right foundation from the start rather than meeting a surprise halfway down a trench.

planning.title: Planning permission for extensions in Essex
planning.intro: This is where local knowledge earns its keep, because Essex is not a single planning authority.
paragraphs: Householder planning is handled by your district, borough or city council, not by Essex County Council. That means Epping Forest, Brentwood, Chelmsford, Uttlesford, Harlow and so on, each with its own local plan. Southend-on-Sea and Thurrock are separate unitary councils. Worth knowing: from April 2028 these councils are being replaced by five new unitary authorities, and Epping Forest, which covers Buckhurst Hill, Chigwell and Loughton, becomes part of West Essex Council. The rules will not change overnight, but the name on the letterhead will.
Many extensions fall under permitted development and need no application, but large parts of Essex carry protections that reduce or remove those rights:

The Metropolitan Green Belt covers much of south and west Essex, including the Epping Forest district. In the Green Belt you can still extend, but the scale is limited, so the work is not a disproportionate addition to the original house.
Conservation areas, which nearly every Essex town and village has, restrict what you can do without permission.
The Dedham Vale National Landscape in the north east, the protected area formerly known as an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and Epping Forest in the south west both add a further layer.
Listed buildings, of which Essex has more than fourteen thousand, need separate consent.

One Essex particular: most councils here treat the Essex Design Guide as a material consideration, so a scheme that ignores its standards on space, light and character can meet resistance. We design with all of this in mind, work out early whether your project needs permission, and prepare and manage the application where it does.

cost.title: What does an extension cost in Essex?
paragraphs: The honest answer is that it depends on size, specification, ground conditions and finish.

As a general guide for this part of the country, single storey extensions commonly run at a few thousand pounds per square metre of finished space, with double storey often better value per square metre and high specifications sitting above the base. Protected settings, sloping plots and difficult ground can add to the groundwork. Treat those figures as a starting point, not a quote.
For an early estimate you can use our cost calculator, and for a real figure the best step is a site visit where we price the actual project.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for an extension in Essex?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Many extensions fall under permitted development, but the Green Belt, conservation areas, the Dedham Vale National Landscape, Epping Forest and listed status all restrict those rights. It depends on your property and which district or borough council covers it. We check this for you early.

faqs.q: Which council handles my extension application in Essex?
faqs.a: Your local district, borough or city council, such as Epping Forest, Brentwood or Chelmsford, not Essex County Council. Southend-on-Sea and Thurrock have their own unitary councils. From April 2028 these are being replaced by five new unitary authorities. We deal with the right authority for your address.

faqs.q: How much does a house extension cost in Essex?
faqs.a: It depends on size, specification and ground conditions. As a rough guide, single storey extensions commonly run at a few thousand pounds per square metre, but the only accurate figure comes from a site visit. Our cost calculator gives an early estimate.

faqs.q: How do I get a quote for my extension?
faqs.a: Call us on 07920 731533 or send the enquiry form. We arrange a free, no-obligation site visit, then give you a clear, itemised written quote for the actual project.

faqs.q: Do you handle the planning and building regulations for me?
faqs.a: Yes. We manage the planning application, building control and any party wall notices, so you are not dealing with councils and paperwork on your own.

faqs.q: Which parts of Essex do you cover?
faqs.a: We work across the county, with a focus on the south west, including Buckhurst Hill, Chigwell, Loughton, Epping, Ongar, Brentwood and Chelmsford, and we travel for the right project. Contact us to confirm your area.
